💡 Key Takeaways
  • B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.
  • The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.
  • B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla.

B2 Architecture has created the Life Behind the Walls exhibition in Prague, using a maze of red timber frames and translucent fabric to explore life in North Korea.

The 1,500-square-metre exhibition takes visitors from a bright, interactive installation designed around a children’s book to a darkened gallery featuring portraits and testimonies from North Korean defectors.

B2 Architecture divided the installation into two contrasting environments. The first features a grid of red-painted timber beams, with large sheets of red and pink fabric suspended between the frames to create semi-transparent walls.

The structure forms a maze that visitors can explore, with glimpses of other rooms and activities visible through the fabric.

Illustrated panels, games and interactive activities are fitted into the structure, while photographs by photographer Michal Huniewicz show North Korea as it is presented to the outside world.

Children are encouraged to navigate the maze independently and stop to draw, write and complete activities as they move through the installation.

The displays are based on Tota lítá, a children’s book by North Korean studies scholar and writer Nina Špitálníková, which explains the principles of totalitarianism in language that is accessible to younger readers.

“Children are often given very little space within exhibition formats,” B2 Architecture told Dezeen. “This project consciously challenges that convention.”.

The atmosphere changes as visitors pass between two walls displaying photographs of the border between North Korea and China by photographer Tim Franco.

Industry observers note that beyond this threshold, the playful red maze gives way to a dark gallery. This contains black display structures with portraits and personal accounts of people who escaped North Korea, alongside stories of those who did not survive its regime.

Tall, translucent fabric panels printed with shadowy human figures were arranged throughout the space, creating silhouettes that overlap with the portraits displayed behind them.

In a central room, a monumental statue of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un stands on a raised plinth, surrounded by spotlights and theatrical mist.

The temporary installation was constructed using lightweight, modular timber beams and stretched textiles, allowing it to be assembled and dismantled efficiently.

The timber structure was retained for use in another project, while the textiles and flooring were passed on to several theatres for reuse.

Prague-based B2 Architecture was founded by architect Barbara Bencová in 2012 and works across residential and commercial architecture, interiors and public spaces.

Other projects by the studio featured on Dezeen include the DDB Prague office, which features an anamorphic optical illusion that makes the advertising agency’s logo appear complete from a particular viewpoint.

Photography by Radek Šrettr Úlehla.

Say What? 7 Tips to Unclog Your Blocked Ears

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1280 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears.
  • According to recent reports, whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort.
  • According to recent reports, clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure might be behind your clogged ears. There are many easy ways to get relief at home. Whether it’s from a cold, allergies, or changes in air pressure, blocked ears can disrupt your day-to-day activities and even cause discomfort. Thankfully, there are several effective methods to help unclog your ears and restore your hearing. Listen up! Why are my ears clogged? Clogging can happen either on the inside or the outside of your eardrum. Here are the most common ways your ears can get blocked: Earwax in the outer ear helps prevent particles and excess water from entering the middle ear. However, if earwax builds up too much outside the eardrum, it can cause a blockage. If you’ve been swimming recently, some water might be stuck in your ear canal, pushing against your eardrum. When that water hangs around too long, it can lead to a swimmer’s ear, an outer ear infection. Sinus infections, ear infections, and Eustachian tube dysfunction can pressure your eardrum’s inner side. Allergies can cause uncomfortable inflammation and congestion in your ears. Your sinuses, throat, and ears are connected, so when you feel stuffed up and sniffly, your inner ear feels the pain too. Changes in air pressure, like when you fly, can cause uncomfortable ear pressure. Best clogged ear remedies 1. Pop and unclog The easiest way to unclog your ears is by “popping” them. Just pinch your nose shut, seal your lips, and gently blow. This simple technique, known as the Valsalva maneuver, won’t clear earwax or fluid but is a common trick people use on planes. 2. Swallow, yawn, or chew The Eustachian tubes connect your middle ear to the back of your throat. They briefly open when you swallow, yawn, or chew. Altitude changes can cause these tubes to close, but chewing gum or yawning can help reopen them. Alternatively, you can try the Toynbee maneuver, where you hold your nose and swallow. 3. Ear drops Over-the-counter (OTC) ear drops can soften and dissolve excess earwax. If you prefer a DIY approach, warm a small amount of mineral oil and use an eye dropper to apply a few drops into your ear for a few minutes. Pro tip: Baby oil or olive oil can also be used, but make sure it’s not too hot. Additionally, diluted hydrogen peroxide drops can be helpful. 4. Warmth and gravity To loosen up clogged earwax, use a warm, damp washcloth as a compress. Lie down with the clogged ear facing down against the heated washcloth. Gravity and heat will help the earwax move along more easily. 5. Hit the steam room Steam can help drain sinuses and alleviate pressure in your inner ear. Close the bathroom door, let the hot shower run for a while, and then luxuriate with deep, cleansing breaths. 6. Take allergy medication Because your throat, sinuses, and ears are interconnected, any sickness affecting your sinuses or throat can also impact your ears. Over-the-counter antihistamines, decongestants, or nasal sprays can relieve sniffles, coughs, and ear discomfort. 7. Rinse away the gunk Rinsing your nasal passages with a medication-free saline solution can help reduce congestion and clear out mucus that might be causing ear blockage. You can also consider investing in a nasal irrigation system for more thorough mucus clearing. When to see your doctor Have you been unable to unclog your ears for a few days, or are you experiencing severe pain, fever, dizziness, hearing loss, fluid discharge, or unusual odor? If so, it’s crucial to contact your healthcare provider promptly. These symptoms may indicate an infection that needs medical attention. What not to do when you have clogged ears Cotton swabs: Q-tips and other cotton swabs to remove earwax can push it further into your ear canal, so don’t do it. Candling: Ear candles might seem like a fun party trick, but there’s no science to prove they work, and they’ve been shown to cause injuries. Sprays: Decongestant nasal sprays can be helpful, but using them too long can lead to rebound congestion. Drying solutions: A few drops of rubbing alcohol or a mixture of one part vinegar and one part alcohol can help dry out the ears when you have a swimmer’s ear. However, doing this regularly can lead to irritation. Takeaway Clogged ears are often caused by earwax buildup, allergies, infections, or changes in air pressure. You can use over-the-counter or DIY ear drops, irrigation kits, or warm compresses to unblock your ears. Antihistamines or nasal sprays can also help relieve clogs caused by allergies. PSA: Consult a healthcare provider if your blocked ears are painful or at-home remedies don’t work.

#103016. 15 Van Gogh Masterpieces that Set Auction Records

15 Van Gogh Masterpieces that Set Auction Records

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2354 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in 1990 Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr.
  • Below are 15 of the Dutch master’s most remarkable paintings, each of which has achieved a place among the highest prices for a Van Gogh in auction history.
  • A version of this article was first published on May 19, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in 1990 Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr. Gachet stunned the art world when it soared to $82.5 million at Christie’s New York, setting a new record for any painting at auction at the time. It was one of several headline-grabbing sales that cemented Van Gogh as one of the market’s most coveted names. From swirling fields and blazing cypresses painted in Saint-Rémy to delicate still lifes and portraits from Arles and Auvers-sur-l’Oise, Van Gogh’s works continue to captivate collectors and institutions alike. Today his canvases routinely fetch eight-figure sums, driven by their emotional intensity and storied provenance.

Below are 15 of the Dutch master’s most remarkable paintings, each of which has achieved a place among the highest prices for a Van Gogh in auction history.

A version of this article was first published on May 19, 2026. It was last updated on November 20, 2026.

According to recent reports, on May 13, 2021, Christie’s New York auctioned Van Gogh’sBridge at Trinquetaille, completed in June 1888 during his productive Arles period. The painting achieved $37.4 million, including buyer’s premium, surpassing its pre-sale high estimate of $35 million. It depicts the road bridge to Trinquetaille across the Rhône River, near the house where Van Gogh lived for a time with Paul Gauguin. Notably, Van Gogh described the sky and river as “the color of absinthe,” a striking greenish yellow, reflecting his bold palette and emotional intensity. The scene includes figures that the painter called “ruffians of the Rue du bout d’Arles,” referencing the town’s red-light district. After his death, the painting passed through the hands of several owners, including his brother Theo, the British art collector Elizabeth Workman, and Saudi businessman Akram Ojjeh. The painting is currently held in a private collection.

According to recent reports, this work from one of Van Gogh’s celebrated Sunflowers series of 1888 sold for approximately $39.9 million at Christie’s London on March 31, 1987, a record at the time for any painting sold at auction. The buyer was Yasuda Fire & Marine Insurance Co. of Japan (now Sompo), which donated the painting to the Sompo Museum of Art in Tokyo, where it remains today. Executed in vibrant yellows with expressive brushwork, the painting was created to decorate Van Gogh’s house in Arles before a visit by Paul Gauguin, symbolizing the artist’s optimism and creative aspirations during this fertile period in the South of France.

It has been revealed that this canvas, painted in 1890 during Van Gogh’s final months in Auvers-sur-Oise, depicts a seated woman against a backdrop of wheat stalks and poppies. The muted color palette and contemplative mood mark a departure from the artist’s earlier, more turbulent portraits. American casino magnate Stephen A. Wynn made news when he acquired the painting in 1997 for $47.8 million; in 2025 Wynn sold it privately, along with a painting by Paul Gaugin, to hedge fund manager Steven A. Cohen for a combined price of more than $100 million. These private transactions underscore Van Gogh’s enduring prominence and appeal in the art market, particularly for works from the last two years of his life.

On April 24, 1985, Van Gogh’s Landscape with Rising Sun, created in 1889 during his yearlong stay at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, sold for $9.9 million at Sotheby’s Latest York. This sale established a record for Impressionist and Post-Impressionist works, exceeding the previous Van Gogh auction high of $5.7 million. The painting portrays a wheat field in the early morning, viewed from the artist’s room on the first floor of the hospital. Before Florence J. Gould purchased it in 1965, the work was owned by physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who inherited it from his father Julius, a Viennese collector. The painting was among the earliest Van Gogh works exhibited internationally and was part of the Museum of Modern Art’s first exhibition in 1929. Despite initial doubts about its market appeal, the sale underscored growing enthusiasm for Van Gogh’s landscapes and signaled a turning point in the valuation of his art.

Industry observers note that van Gogh’s Fields near Les Alpilles (1889) sold for $52 million at Christie’s in Latest York on May 12, 2022. Painted near the asylum at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, the work depicts a wheat field with lilac mountains behind it and a solitary almond tree in its center. The tree’s stark outline suggests Van Gogh’s admiration for Japanese prints. Until the sale, it had long been hidden in private collections, including that of it fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent and his partner Pierre Bergé, who had farmhouses near Saint-Rémy named after Van Gogh. It is rightly celebrated for its vivid brushwork and evocative colors capturing late autumn in the French countryside.

In a recent development, on November 11, 1987, Sotheby’s Newly introduced York auctioned Irises, painted in May 1889 within days of Van Gogh’s voluntary admission to the Saint-Rémy-de-Provence asylum. The hammer dropped at $49 million, with a 10 percent commission bringing the total to $53.9 million. The winning bidder turned out to be Australian businessman Alan Bond, who was unable to complete the transaction. The painting was acquired for an undisclosed sum about three years later by the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles, where it remains today. Previously it had been in the collection of Joan Whitney Payson. Its bold colors and fluid brushwork mark a pivotal moment in Van Gogh’s artistic recovery, reflecting the emotional intensity and renewed vitality he found in nature during his time at the asylum. The dramatic sale drew a packed house and global media attention, cementing the ascendance of Van Gogh as a market titan.

It has been revealed that van Gogh’s Landscape Under a Stormy Sky was painted in April 1889 in Arles and sold for $54 million at Sotheby’s, Latest York, on November 5, 2015. It was completed a few months after Van Gogh famously mutilated his ear in December 1888 and shortly before he admitted himself to the asylum at Saint-Rémy. The painting depicts a meadow filled with spring flowers, with a man and a woman walking on the left beneath heavy grey clouds. It was one of the last landscapes Van Gogh painted in Arles and is referred to in his letters to his brother Theo in mid-April 1889 as one of six spring studies. The canvas was later retrieved from Arles and sent to Theo in Paris in July. The sky, painted in thick expressive strokes, is unusual in Van Gogh’s Arles work and may reflect the difficult circumstances of his final months there.

It has been revealed that on November 4, 2014, Van Gogh’s Still Life, Vase with Daisies and Poppies, completed in June 1890 just weeks before his death, achieved $61.8 million at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its estimate by over $10 million. The artist created this dramatic and colorful canvas while staying at the home of his physician, Dr. Paul Gachet. Garchet was an art collector and amateur painter, and Van Gogh is thought to have drawn inspiration from some of the works in the doctor’s house, including Cezanne’s flower paintings. He may even have given the still life in exchange for treatment.

This rare piece is one of the few Van Gogh paintings sold during his lifetime. It later entered the collection of Conger Goodyear, a founder of the Museum of Modern Art, before moving through private hands and being exhibited at the Albright Knox Art Gallery for over 30 years. The buyer was Chinese billionaire and entertainment mogul Wang Zhongjun, an amateur artist with a fondness for flower-filled compositions. This sale reflects a shift in the Van Gogh market, with East Asian collectors—especially in China.

In a recent development, van Gogh’s The Avenue of Les Alyscamps was painted in November 1888 during his time in Arles, shortly after his friend Paul Gauguin came to stay with him. The work depicts in vibrant colors the central thoroughfare of the ancient Roman burial ground at Alyscamps, near Arles. It was created during a brief period of collaboration between the two artists, who captured the site, each from different viewpoints. After years in private collections, the painting was sold at Christie’s in Latest York on May 12, 2003, for $12 million. When it returned to auction at Sotheby’s New York on November 10, 2015, it fetched $66 million. The buyer was officially anonymous, though believed to be a Chinese collector. This dramatic increase reflects the continuing high demand for Van Gogh’s art.

According to recent reports, completed in 1889 at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, Wood Cabins Among the Olive Trees and Cypresses showcases Van Gogh’s distinctive impasto technique, depicting two modest buildings in vibrant natural surroundings. This pastoral scene reflects the artist’s deep connection to the Provençal landscape during his prolific asylum period. The painting fetched $71.35 million at Christie’s New York on November 11, 2021, highlighting sustained collector enthusiasm for Van Gogh’s landscapes. Until then, it had been held in the collection of the Texas oilman Edwin Cox.

Painted in September 1889 at the asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, this work is one of the few self-portraits in which Van Gogh appears with no facial hair. Created shortly after he shaved his beard, it may have been intended as a gift for his mother to show that he was in better health. The intense blue-green background, combined with his direct, piercing gaze, gives the painting a raw emotional power that distinguishes the artist’s late works. Executed with his signature impasto technique, the canvas reflects both vulnerability and resolve during a fraught period in the artist’s life. It achieved $71.5 million at Christie’s New York in November 19, 1998. The work had previously been held in the collection of German entrepreneur Jacques Koerfer and was rarely exhibited, adding to its desirability.

Painted in early September 1889 during Van Gogh’s stay at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, Laborer in a Field features a lone peasant working beneath a vast, swirling sky. After a devastating epileptic episode that kept him away from painting for more than six weeks, Van Gogh returned to his brushes with renewed vigor and hope, using the view from his room—a wheat field enclosed by a stone wall—as inspiration. The painting’s earth tones and rhythmic brushwork capture not only its subject’s labor but also the artist’s own struggle toward creative and emotional renewal. This work, painted during one of the most turbulent yet fruitful periods of Van Gogh’s life, sold for $81.3 million at Christie’s Newly introduced York on November 13, 2017, having passed through the estate of billionaire collectors Nancy Lee and Perry R. Bass. The painting’s return to the market after decades away attracted strong collector interest, reflecting both its artistic and historical significance.

Industry observers note that completed in Auvers-sur-Oise shortly before Van  Gogh’s death, Portrait of Dr. Gachet (1890) was hammered down for $82.5 million at Sotheby’s New York on May 16, 1990, setting a world auction record at the time. The buyer was Japanese businessman Ryoei Saito, who claimed he intended to have the painting cremated with him upon his death. This depiction of Dr. Paul Gachet, Van Gogh’s physician, reveals him resting his head on one hand, surrounded by foxglove flowers and books. Its emotional intensity and the limited availability of works by the artist made it one of the most coveted Van Gogh portraits ever to appear on the market. After Saito’s death, in 1996, the painting’s whereabouts become uncertain. Reports suggest that it was sold to Austrian-born investment manager Wolfgang Flöttl in 1997 or 1998, but the current owner and location of the painting remain unknown.

Orchard with Cypresses (1888), painted during Van Gogh’s prolific Arles period, sold for $117.2 million at Christie’s Upcoming York on November 10, 2022, setting a record for the artist that still stands. The canvas portrays a vibrant Provençal landscape with twisting olive trees, dark cypresses, and a luminous sky rendered in thick, energetic brushstrokes. Before its record-breaking sale, the work was part of the collection owned by Paul G. Allen, the Microsoft cofounder. Its well-preserved condition, coupled with an exceptional provenance, contributed to its historic result at auction.

On November 18, 2026, Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), a picture of sunlit trees set against oncoming storm clouds, sold for $190.4 million (including fees) at Sotheby’s. The cover lot for the auction house’s Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” it set a new auction record for the Dutch painter. The reported buyer was dealer William Acquavella.

The artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold for $102 million. The upcoming result beat that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

According to recent reports, that the sale happened at all was a victory for Sotheby’s. Just days before the auction, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement, clearing the painting’s title.

Painted shortly after Van Gogh arrived at Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Blossoming Chestnut Trees is among the 70-plus paintings (and more than 50 drawings) that the artist made there before taking his own life only two months later. It was also one of only eight Auvers landscapes still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper.

Sources indicate that the electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades. It was last exhibited at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in 1964 before Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro and Nelly Arrieta Blaquier, bought it in 1975—the kind of provenance and scarcity that fuels record-breaking prices like this one.—Daniel Cassady.

#103015. Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1399 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Eight highlights from this year's Sharjah Architecture Triennial

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology.
  • Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.
  • Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The third Sharjah Architecture Triennial focuses on the myriad ways architecture can be understood through the lens of anthropology. Here are our highlights from the event, including installations and exhibitions.

Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao, this year’s edition was centred on the theme Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures.

Rao said the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which takes place over five months, will invite discourse about the different ways cities and urban life can be imagined.

“Though I’m not an architect, I’m literally talking to students day in and day out about how they see the world, and how that translates into the practice,” Rao told Dezeen.

Sources indicate that “Being an academic, you’re always asked to define yourself in terms of your discipline,” she continued. “It doesn’t make sense to limit yourself, especially when you are in the practice of life.”.

“You’re learning from people about the ways in which they live – that’s what I do as an anthropologist, and I think that’s what a lot of architects do because they’re inspired to build for people and the places that they inhabit and thrive in.”.

Read on for eight highlights from this year’s Sharjah Architecture Triennial.

Open the School by Curry J Hackett.

Artist Curry J Hackett created this draping shelter spanning the width of the Old Al Jubail Vegetable Market in homage to the Black community in Virginia’s Prince Edward County, which created improvised learning spaces when schools closed during the Civil Rights Movement.

Videos play in the former stalls at either end of the fabric enclosure, screening archival images of the period, as well as images of Rosenwald Schools – the community-building initiative that established thousands of schools for Black children in the South.

It has been revealed that “Rather than integrate, schools closed for five years, and leading up to that, schools were dealing with a lot of overcrowding,” Hackett told Dezeen. “The county begrudgingly funded ‘tar paper shacks’, which were shoddy, demoralising structures, to ease overcrowding, and that’s what you’re seeing interpreted here,” he continued.

“Interspersed sonically and visually throughout the installation is a mashing up of the local story of my home town in Virginia with the regional story of the Rosenwald Schools in the South – their architectural rethinking of materials and retelling the history.”.

Research and construction studio Abari showcased a tent-like structure made from a bamboo frame, which was limited in size due to difficulties with material regulations.

The structure is one module of a larger pavilion that was constructed in Nepal, designed as a travelling venue to host bamboo weaving workshops.

“We were not able to create an installation here in the UAE, partly because Abari’s work is based on building with bamboo, and the difficulty with this project was that the global supply chain and its regulations could not be met within the timeframe,” remarked Rao.

“What you see here is one repeatable module of a pavilion that is right now moving within different communities in Nepal – we improvised and decided Sharjah would travel to Nepal, and we’d just have a piece of it here in this exhibition.”.

Sabeel Negotiated by Samar Halloum.

Drawing upon her fieldwork in Sharjah, Palestinian architect Samar Halloum designed a brick pavilion that was shaded overhead by a draping fabric canopy.

In reference to the historical public drinking-water structures in the Gulf region, Sabeel Negotiated features a water fountain and wooden stools for people to gather around.

According to Rao, the strikes by Iran on countries in the Middle East in February disrupted brick supply in the United Arab Emirates, so Halloum redesigned the pavilion with cloth-filled bricks.

It has been revealed that “One of the shortages was bricks because they come from Saudi Arabia, and the factory stopped producing bricks,” said Rao. “There were some leftover bales of cloth from another installation, so Halloum used those bales and cast them in resin, so you’ll see some of the bricks in the installation are actually made of cloth.”.

History as Repair: Documenting Karachi by Kishwar Rizvi.

This exhibition by art historian Kishwar Rizvi explores how colonised communities in Karachi, Pakistan, took ownership of their urban environment by adapting architectural styles, from European classicism to Mughal-inspired ornament.

Through maps, photographs, sketches and interviews, it aims to shine a light on an architectural history at risk of being forgotten.

The exhibition argues for the protection of colonial-era buildings in Karachi, which are under threat of demolition due to neglect.

Patch-Time by Hiba Bou Akar, Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb.

The Patch-Time installation is a collaboration between architect Hiba Bou Akar and artists Mohamad Hafeda and Nathalie Harb that explores the displacement of people in Lebanon, from the 1970s to the present day, through the materials used to protect and repair homes.

In workshops organised by the Patch-Time team with Lebanese non-profit Ahla Fawda, displaced women crocheted tarpaulin, sand-bag cloth and sheeting into panels that form a canopy displayed in a courtyard at the triennial’s Al Qasimiyah School venue.

Underneath the canopy, a table made from breeze blocks, wood and a central mirror displays fabric artwork and the stories of women and children affected by war.

Industry observers note that “We worked on two levels: one that is the collective, and one that is more of the individual, looking at how people shelter their home through war adversity and displacement,” said Harb. “We asked [the women] what their relationship to their home was, and in the pieces, you see how it changes from generation to generation with their relationship to material.”.

After Night There is Nothing by Mohamad Nahleh and Ozayr Saloojee.

Architect Mohamad Nahleh and architecture professor Ozayr Saloojee designed a giant globe of the night sky and split it into three parts, which were scattered across different locations at the triennale.

The outer shells of the curved structures are wrapped in thatch, while the interiors feature vinyl surfaces with designs showing man-made military objects in the sky reimagined as creature-like constellations.

“This is ‘night sky optimism’ – optimism through catastrophe,” remarked Nahleh. “The night sky we are talking about in this project is not the sky of beautiful stars and constellations, but the contemporary sky filled with drones, satellites, rockets and missiles that are changing the way we understand the sky above us.”.

Industry observers note that “We have noticed in our research that, especially in geographies witnessing prolonged violence, these objects are producing new mythical creatures,” he continued. “We think of these creatures as ones that attempt to tame the military brightness that is populating the sky around us.”.

As the Sun Rests by Badriyah Alsalem.

Kuwaiti designer Badriyah Alsalem plotted 41 medieval Arabic poetic names for the sun as cut-outs on the astronomical graph that forms a circular canopy over her pavilion, As the Sun Rests.

Forming patterns of shadow in the sand below, three of the suns were embroidered in red, depicting the sharaq rising sun, saqa’a noon sun and gharab setting sun, while markers on the ground show where these canopy highlights will fall on different dates during the triennial.

“If you look up, you see the static data visualisation, and if you look down, it is animated by the sun itself, so it becomes an analogue device to read this historical data,” noted Alsalem.

Lalla Alwyia Khalwa by Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.

Situated on Sharjah’s Al Khan Open Beach, Lalla Alwyia Khalwa is an installation designed as a place for reflection away from the busy city, dedicated to the saint Lalla Alwyia Kasserine.

Dried plants form a grid of columns on a raised platform for visitors to walk through. Stone slabs on the floor mark places of pause, and a metal stool provides a reflective space to listen to the accompanying sound installation.

“We chose the beach because it is already a space for retreat, so this is a retreat inside a retreat,” stated the design team, Ziad Jamaleddine, Makram el Kadi, Iheb Guermazi and Beya Othmani.

“We carved a series of spaces – one for prayer, one for sitting, and a courtyard to enjoy the sky.”.

Sharjah Architecture Triennial 2026 takes place from 14 November 2026 to 14 April 2027 at various locations across Sharjah, UAE. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

In a recent development, tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:.

According to recent reports, tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:.

According to recent reports, tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

According to recent reports, want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Sources indicate that are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Industry observers note that flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related problems and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

According to recent reports, from giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best environmental storytelling in video games doesn’t always hit you in the face and demand you stop to look, and GTA 6 has perfected that. Sometimes it’s a carefully dressed room, an overgrown garden, or a detail you spot out of the corner of your eye while heading somewhere else.

Industry observers note that rockstar’s developers say that kind of discovery is central to Grand Theft Auto 6, a world designed to reward players who take their time. After three weeks of playing GTA 6, I'd say the world-building is some of the best, most detailed, and most nuanced I've experienced. It can be as small as mud on a character's trainers, a branded coffee mug, or a car decal.

It has been revealed that “The life is in the detail of Grand Theft Auto VI,” notes Adam Cochrane, Vice President of Art: Environment. “The subtle sway of trees or bunting swaying in the wind. A puddle of bin juice around the bottom of a dumpster, or an overgrown garden in a property that is unoccupied.”.

It’s the sort of detail that makes a place feel inhabited rather than assembled for a game. Cochrane points to the personalisation of homes and businesses, and the little vignettes the teams have added for players to discover. Some offer in-game rewards; others are there simply to be found.

It has been revealed that “Then you zoom out, and you look at the sheer scale of the world, and you realise that the detail you’ve been discovering on such a small scale is quite literally everywhere across the vast landscape of this world,” he indicates. “Then you realise that it’s all been curated, considered, and created by a human hand, and you can’t quite believe it.”.

It has been revealed that that thinking extends beyond what you can see. Steven Messinger, Senior Design Director: Open World, explains that Rockstar has built deep backstories for things players may only glimpse. The game’s gang compounds, for example, have a fully mapped drug network, from supply routes to street-level buyers.

“Players will only pick up on bits and pieces of this,” Messinger says, “but having that structure in the background as something we consistently refer to helps everything feel more real, like this big machine is always running even when players aren’t there.”.

It’s a huge amount of work for details many players may miss. That’s rather the point.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite the contemporary art world’s increased attention to women’s experiences and the politics of care in its public-facing programming, working mothers employed by London’s galleries and auction houses face widespread discrimination, according to a fresh study. As reported by the Art Newspaper today, a survey of 50 employees working in the UK capital’s commercial art sector has found that, for many, having children comes at considerable professional cost.

According to recent reports, the study, conducted by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi and published today in the European Journal of Cultural Studies, looked at the extent to which pregnancy and maternity affected career progression among art world workers. Moving beyond previous studies centered on fine artists or senior directors, it focused on lower-paid, non-artist roles such as sales, administration, and marketing. Related Articles Recent Key Departures at Phillips Point to a Pivot in Strategy The Year in Gallery Closures: A Collapse or a Transition to a Smarter Market?

Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s research, which also included 12 in-depth interviews, reveals an industry “marred by implicit and explicit expectations that often result in workers needing to choose between their careers and being parents,” they write. Three quarters of respondents felt that motherhood had impeded career advancement, while 20 percent stated they had been explicitly denied promotion.

The authors found poor and sometimes illegal practices across the industry, including employees being “managed” out of their roles while on maternity leave. Such practices, they note, are made possible by a lack of formal human resource structures—only half of the respondence worked for organizations with dedicated HR staff, and just 60 percent said their workplace had a specific parental leave policy. They additionally blamed the art market’s pervasive culture of secrecy.

It has been revealed that class and wealth also play a role in shaping employee experience, the study suggests. For junior employees on modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make travel and attendance at evening events difficult and increase the likelihood of discrimination on the job. At the same time, a lack of resources makes challenging such discrimination daunting, with many women instead choosing to take a less senior position, move into freelance work, or leave the art world.

According to recent reports, roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s study spanned small galleries to multinational auction houses and found problems across the board. As they say in their report, “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”.

When I first heard the HEDDphone D1 last November, I said that the German audio company had cracked the code. It's why they remain my top pick of the best-sounding wired, over-ear headphones at any price.

In a recent development, sure, the HEDDphone D1 pack world-first driver technology and are hand-built in Germany, but for me that's not the main pull. It's the sound these things make! If you want neutral, balanced, slightly lean and mean but with exquisite detail, they're the best option at £599 – and a steal at £499!

If you do get the HEDDphone D1 it's worth getting a quality headphone stand too. And you really don't have to spend loads of money to get a good-quality, handsome, wooden stand. For me a good option is the Linkidea wooden stand. Even when it's not discounted, under £30 is a bargain.

Recent findings suggest that usually I don't pay the marketing hype much time, but I make an exception with the HEDDphone D1. That's because they offer the world’s first dynamic driver headphone with a Thin-Ply Carbon Diaphragm (TPCD). Developed in partnership with Swedish material specialists Composite Sound, this aerospace-grade tech controls resonance structurally, eliminating the need for normal driver damping (and the compromises that that method invariably brings). What that all means for me and you is fast transients, and excellent clarity. These things are detailed!

It has been revealed that at 350g, they are lightweight for this tier of headphone – audiophile headphones can get heavy at around the £500 mark. With an impedance of 32ohms and 100dB sensitivity, they're easy to drive – including with inexpensive dongle DACs.

This is a genuinely special headphone, and a decent Black Friday price.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a newly introduced romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

Industry observers note that from those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:.

In a recent development, welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

Industry observers note that if the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the problems head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

Sources indicate that you know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Recent findings suggest that every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Papa Omotayo, Gemma Sfeir and Nifemi Marcus-Bello have helped design two spaces in Lagos for the local creative studio Casa Mouda to host exhibitions that promote design in West Africa.

Casa Mouda’s initiative includes the launch of an exhibition to mark the opening of two spaces in Lagos – aiMe Gallery at Eko Hotel and aiMe Concept on Eko Atlantic.

AiMe Gallery was redesigned by Lagos-based architect Omotayo at the entrance to the hotel’s conference centre, while aiMe Concept was designed with interior designer Sfeir and designer Marcus-Bello in a storefront in the larger Eko Atlantic development.

Both spaces feature exposed concrete walls and columns with touches of warmth, including an earthen bar and screen in aiMe Gallery.

Casa Mouda founder Caline Chagoury Moudaber stated that the spaces, together, were designed to highlight the work done by designers in Lagos.

“As we began to conceive our first chapter of Casa Mouda, we knew we needed to start by recognizing some of the people who had already built so much of its foundation,” remarked Chagoury Moudaber.

“There are incredible designers producing on the continent that have done extraordinary work, often taking on alone what usually takes an entire industry elsewhere.”.

The inaugural exhibitions include designers from Lagos, but also those who have chosen to work in the city from abroad.

Among the latter group is American designer Germane Barnes, who showcased his wooden Corona Chair, which features inverted pyramidal legs, and his take on a peacock chair, both produced in Lagos in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

Beyond his contribution to the interior layout, which includes permanent seating for the hospitality at aiMe Concept, Marcus-Bello showcased his LM stools and M2 shelves. The works showcase the production possible in Lagos, but also a more modern, minimalist angle for Marcus-Bello, who is known for his massive metal collectible design pieces.

“Nifemi Marcus-Bello has been quietly doing the legwork to set up real pathways for production for years,” said Chagoury Moudaber.

On the more craft-oriented side, the collection showcased works in bronze and wood by craftsman Jean Servais Somian, also produced in collaboration with Casa Mouda.

In a recent development, servais Somian’s work includes an armoire with gridded screen wooden doors, a console with stacked oval shelves, stools in wood with painted recesses that have a graphic appearance and textural cast bronze stools and side tables. It is an impressive array showcasing the craftsman’s range.

French studio Hall Haus showcased its metal basketball hoops and chairs, a blend of African aesthetics with Parisian urban ephemera, reflecting the cross-cultural background of the studio’s members.

Meanwhile, Moroccan designer Hajar Daide showcased a mix of delicate Nigerian woven wood techniques with lush blue Moroccan fabrics for her Friction Bench.

Atmosphere was top of mind for the designers, and Casa Mouda worked with US musician Malloy James to create custom speakers at the entryway for aiMe Gallery, while aiMe Concept features a listening station.

The spaces have also been set up to further promote craft in the region through display and retail, such as textiles, bags and other smaller items such as jewellery.

“The designers who have forged the way are sharing information on what they have learned; the ones latest to this area of production are bringing new techniques and perspectives,” mentioned Chagoury Moudaber.

“It has been an incredibly collaborative, generous, and inspiring process – and we are only just beginning.”.

Other recent design showcases include the inaugural Walker Design Triennial in Minnesota and Danish design initiative The Mindcraft Project, curated by Christian + Jade.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Latest York judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit over a 15th-century Fra Angelico painting that the heirs to the Bic pen fortune say was stolen by their family chauffeur and later sold by the late art dealer Richard Feigen.

It has been revealed that in a decision dated October 26 and filed on November 16, Newly introduced York Supreme Court Justice James G. Clynes rejected an attempt by Feigen’s estate and associated businesses to get the case dismissed. Their main argument? The family had waited too long to sue.

“No family should lose a treasured work of art simply because the people who handled this stolen property were sophisticated dealmakers,” Luke Nikas, a lawyer for the Bich family, told ARTnews. The Bich family is determined to recover what belongs to them, and today’s decision is an important step toward achieving that result.” The ruling is good news for the Bich heirs, though there’s still a long way to go. The judge hasn’t decided who owns the painting, or even whether it was stolen. Related Articles Adam Lindemann Sued by Nature Conservancy for Allegedly Installing Julian Schnabel Sculpture Without Permission Fra Angelico's Restored Fiesole Altarpiece Returns to Its Original Church Home After Blockbuster Museum Show.

As ARTnews reported in April, the dispute centers on Saint Sixtus (ca. 1453–55), a painting by the Italian Renaissance master that Baron Marcel Bich, the founder of Bic, bought at Sotheby’s in 1972 for £130,000. The painting eventually passed to his son Bruno, who kept it in his Fifth Avenue apartment in Manhattan. Then, around 2006, it disappeared.

In a recent development, according to a lawsuit filed in March by Bruno’s three sons, Gonzalve, Charles, and Guillaume, the family’s chauffeur, Roy Morrow, stole the painting and sold it to Feigen for $3 million. The family notes Morrow had no paperwork proving the painting was his, but Feigen bought it anyway and promptly insured it for $8.5 million, nearly three times what he’d paid.

Feigen, one of New York’s best-known Old Master dealers before his death in 2021, later consigned the painting to Christie’s. In 2018, it was sold for $5.4 million to Chilean billionaire Álvaro Saieh and his wife, Ana Guzmán.

The Bich brothers say they didn’t learn where the painting ended up until 2023. They asked for it back the following year, but Saieh and Guzmán refused. So the brothers sued, demanding the painting’s return, along with damages and money from its sale.

Feigen’s representatives tell a different story. In March, lawyers for his estate told Reuters that Morrow had signed a bill of sale saying he owned the painting. The Saiehs, meanwhile, have mentioned they bought it in good faith, relying on Christie’s research.

Which brings us to the latest ruling.

Feigen’s lawyers argued that the family had simply waited too long to bring its claims. After all, Feigen bought the painting in 2006 and sold it in 2018. The brothers didn’t file their lawsuit until March 2026.

According to recent reports, but stolen art can be a tricky business under New York law. Generally, when someone buys a stolen artwork in good faith, the clock doesn’t start ticking on a claim for its return until the rightful owner demands it back and the buyer refuses.

Recent findings suggest that things get more complicated when someone is accused of knowingly dealing in stolen property. The clock can start earlier, and Clynes said there were too many unanswered questions about Feigen’s purchase to settle the matter now.

The judge also rejected, for now, an argument that the family had dragged its feet for so long that allowing the case to continue would be unfair. Lawyers call that laches. Both arguments can come up again later.

Feigen’s side did score one win. The judge dismissed claims against his revocable trust and its trustees because the family hadn’t shown enough to connect the trust to the money from the painting’s sale. The brothers can bring those claims again if they find more evidence.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:.

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he states.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he indicates.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe claims.

The fresh Grand Theft Auto arrived this week, the messianic reward after 13 long years, offering the best-rendered version of the series’ standing promise: anything, within the scope of its metropolis and the player’s imagination. I watched my cousin paint a house for his avatar’s girlfriend, then hop in a car and drive to the Bass Museum. Or rather, to the Vice City Museum of Art, the faithful replica of it in Vice City, the game’s fictional Miami.

According to recent reports, rockstar teased that Grand Theft Auto VI would boast the franchise’s sharpest graphics yet, and the claim was not exaggerated. The Vice Museum of Art captures the Bass’s signature civic Art Deco style: a pale limestone facade (the real stuff was quarried in the Florida Keys) and, as far as I could tell, even the carved decorative relief around the entry. It’s a far cry from the series’ earliest entries, when a building like this would have been a smooth beige box; here, the facade looks textured. We parked and admired its public art: a riff on Miami Mountain, a tower of boulders by Ugo Rondinone permanently installed in Collins Park, outside the Bass. Part of Rondinone’s “Mountain” series, it’s made of garishly clashing fluorescent rocks stacked high and probably visible from space. The Vice City version has swapped stone for emojis: winking, crying, smiling. Related Articles Art Advisor Sophia Cohen on How the Next Generation of Collectors Is Approaching the Art Market Ireland's Experiment in Paying Artists a Basic Income Is Working as Intended For Artists.

Vice City may be hiding another Easter egg for art heads. Months ago, a screenshot circulated online from an expansion for Grand Theft Auto Online, showing a latest character in a shirt with an “Art Oregano” logo. It’s a safe bet that it’s a nod to Art Basel Miami Beach, held at the Miami Beach Convention Center, since it’s set in the same font as the fair’s. The herby homage was well received. “I hope he’ll be in GTA 6 having his own little art studio or something,” wrote one Reddit user. Another added, “I can’t wait to wear this shirt to Art Basel this year, if I can pull myself away from GTA6.”.

Art Basel Miami Beach runs December 4-6; keep an eye out for Art Oregano shirts. And, perhaps, as players make it further into the notoriously long game, a upcoming version of Art Oregano may appear.

I couldn’t personally verify whether the game includes a replica of the fair, with NPCs entering and exiting, as the Vice Museum did. We’d spent the momentous night mundanely, mostly comparing paint swatches. All of it in line with what viral clips suggest: the game’s characters can do drugs and rob banks—chaos, generally speaking—but we’d rather have time to drive with no destination in mind.

Industry observers note that before I left, my cousin regretfully canceled our prepares to visit the Guggenheim on Saturday. He has to work.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Lv Xiaobin.

Jiang Deng Lu is a house in rural Anhui designed by Chinese studio Shisuo Design Office using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

Described by Shisuo Design Office as a “surreal rural house”, the compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site.

It sits beside the client’s ancestral home and serves as both a memorial for his late father and a separate dwelling where his elderly mother can host visiting relatives.

“The client wanted to build a house beside the old family home, providing a comfortable place for his mother and relatives to gather and share meals during holidays,” Shisuo Design Office told Dezeen.

“But beyond this practical need, there was a deeper emotional connection. The old house was left by his father, while the upcoming one represented his own way of creating new memories for the family,” it continued.

“We hoped the house would bring the family together more often, beyond just festive occasions.”.

Jiang Deng Lu’s proportions were determined by the recycled stainless steel offcuts and unused windows salvaged for the project by the client, who is the owner of a stainless steel factory.

“The building’s geometry was strictly reverse-engineered from these salvaged materials,” stated Shisuo Design Office.

In a recent development, “Instead of imposing a predetermined architectural form, we meticulously measured and mapped these specific surplus components. The building’s precise dimensions, roof pitches, and structural envelope were entirely reverse-engineered from this salvaged inventory,” added the studio.

“The resulting structure starkly contrasts the client’s modern, lightweight metal industry with the heavy, rooted legacy of his father’s masonry, translating familial love into a rigorous tectonic language,” the studio noted.

Recent findings suggest that externally, the house is wrapped in a full stainless-steel facade, which the studio said deliberately contrasts with “traditional rural vernacular”. This is punctured by the salvaged windows, positioned to frame views of the river.

It has a rectangular plan, with a balcony that is suspended over the river on one side.

Industry observers note that inside is a living space, which sits raised above a dining area accessed directly from the foyer. A bathroom and shower room sit off this dining space.

Interior finishes are pared-back, with stone flooring and white walls complementing the cool-toned exterior of the home. Wooden furnishings and greenery seen through the windows add warmth to the space.

According to Shisuo Design Office, the highlight of the interior is a nine-metre-long window that cantilevers 2.2 metres outward, providing shelter for the terrace below.

“The most distinctive feature is a nine-metre-long horizontal window facing east, overlooking a grove of trees planted by the client’s late father,” mentioned the studio.

According to recent reports, “For the client, these trees are more than a landscape; they hold personal memories of his father. We wanted to bring the grove into everyday life, rather than simply frame it as a view.”.

Jiang Deng Lu is shortlisted in the rural house category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Casa Plaj by Extrastudio and Hata-Mazanka Guesthouses by YOD Group.

Another house featured on Dezeen with a distinctive metal facade is Bondi House, a two-storey, two-bedroom dwelling by Nick Kent Design in Sydney.

Photography by Lv Xiaobin.

El Greco Masterpiece Gets Its Colors Back After More Than 400 Years

💡 Key Takeaways
  • King Philip II of Spain wasn’t particularly impressed with El Greco‘s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion when he first saw it.
  • Recent findings suggest that A painstaking nine-month restoration, recently finished, has found the monumental painting looking considerably more like the one El Greco envisioned.
  • The restoration was conducted at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery, under the supervision of Rafael Alonso, an 81-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, who has spent decades working on El Greco’s paintings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

King Philip II of Spain wasn’t particularly impressed with El Greco‘s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion when he first saw it. The following four centuries of dirt, varnish, and enthusiastic repainting hadn’t done the picture any favors, either.

Recent findings suggest that A painstaking nine-month restoration, recently finished, has found the monumental painting looking considerably more like the one El Greco envisioned. The muddy browns and sickly greens that had dulled the picture for generations are gone. In their place are brilliant blues, reds, yellows, and purples, along with a newfound depth that had been buried beneath grime. Related Articles AI Model Reveals Newly introduced Information About Authorship of 17th-Century El Greco Altarpiece 15th-Century Bellini Altarpiece in Venice to Be Restored While the Public Watches.

The restoration was conducted at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery, under the supervision of Rafael Alonso, an 81-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, who has spent decades working on El Greco’s paintings. The project was supported by the Fundacion Callia in partnership with Spain’s Patrimonio Nacional, which oversees the country’s royal collections.

According to recent reports, the results were reported in detail by El País, whose writer followed the restoration from the painting’s removal from El Escorial in February through its finished restoration in October. And what a job it was.

Alonso had initially expected the restoration to take about four months. But once he and fellow restorer Adela Murgui began cleaning the enormous canvas, which measures nearly 15 feet high and 10 feet wide, they discovered that its condition was far worse than even feared.

Sources indicate that “When I put the cotton to the painting, my heart sank,” Alonso told El País. Centuries of varnish and repainting had darkened the colors and flattened the composition. In the 19th century, he explained, painters had simply painted over damaged areas, often adding their own interpretations of what El Greco intended.

Recent findings suggest that the restorers spent months carefully stripping away those additions, revealing the original paint beneath. Afterward, the repaired the damaged areas using soluble materials, taking pains not to add anything that couldn’t be removed later.

The restoration is particularly striking given the painting’s rather unhappy beginnings.

El Greco painted The Martyrdom between 1580 and 1582 for the basilica at El Escorial, Philip II’s vast monastery and palace outside Madrid. The king wanted a powerful statement of Catholic faith, while the artist hoped the commission might secure him a permanent position as a court painter.

Neither’s wish was totally granted.

Rather than concentrate on the grisly execution of Saint Maurice and his fellow Christian soldiers, El Greco pushed the violence into the background. Up front, he placed a group of handsome soldiers in brightly colored clothing, their elongated bodies and theatrical poses exemplary of the skills he had learned in Venice and Rome.

Philip II apparently admired the painting’s quality, paying the artist a substantial sum of 800 ducats, but felt it wasn’t right for its intended religious setting. The work was relegated to another room, and El Greco never clinched the royal appointment he’d hoped for.

The painting stayed there for most of the next 444 years, apart from a trip to Madrid for an exhibition in 1999, all the while gradually losing most of its remarkable color and atmosphere.

The restoration also marks another achievement for the Fundacion Callia, founded by Carmen Reviriego, which has helped restore works by Zurbarán, Rubens, Brueghel the Elder, Velázquez, and others through its partnership with Madrid’s Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando. According to El País, the foundation has helped mobilize €5 million for the preservation of artworks.

Recent findings suggest that when ARTnews spoke with Reviriego in March, she described Callia as an “incubator of patrons,” bringing together collectors and philanthropists from Spain, Latin America, and beyond. Her goal is to encourage a stronger culture of private support for the arts in a country that has traditionally relied heavily on public funding.

Reviriego had specifically mentioned The Martyrdom during that interview as an example of the work the foundation hoped to support. “El Greco was the Jeff Koons or Damien Hirst of his day,” she told ARTnews this week, “and Phillip II was the most power man and greatest patron of the 16th century.”.

According to recent reports, there’s a nice historical symmetry here. Reviriego argued that great works of art are rarely the achievement of an artist alone. Without patrons, many wouldn’t exist at all. She pointed to the Royal Collections themselves, built in part through the patronage of Philip II, the very king who commissioned The Martyrdom more than four centuries ago. Now, private patronage has helped give that painting a new life.

Sources indicate that for Alonso, meanwhile, the completed restoration marks something of a farewell. After decades spent working on El Greco’s paintings, he told El País that The Martyrdom was the last of the artist’s great masterpieces still awaiting restoration.

Industry observers note that the newly restored painting is expected to go on temporary display at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery before returning to El Escorial. This time, visitors will get a much better idea of what Philip II saw more than four centuries ago.

These 8BitDo Tomb Raider controllers have made me rethink collectable gaming hardware

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1029 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I've never really been one for collectable controllers.
  • This is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller.
  • It has been revealed that the controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I've never really been one for collectable controllers. I'm a fairly practical gamer, I suppose, and while I appreciate nice hardware design, I'm usually more interested in how a controller feels than how it looks, whether it has an on-brand D-pad or decals, for example. But opening the Tomb Raider 30th Anniversary Edition of 8BitDo's Ultimate 3 Controller has changed my mind a little, and I think it's largely down to the box.

This is proper packaging design, crafted as much for the fan experience as for protecting the controller. The Ultimate 3's box changes shape, opens, slides and reveals its secrets, almost like Lara Croft discovering some long-lost treasure, and I found myself enjoying the whole process far more than I expected. There's even a little golden envelope, almost hidden away, containing the instructions and a month of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate. It's all very Tomb Raider, and yes, I know I'm getting excited about a cardboard box.

It has been revealed that the controller sits on a sliding shelf, so even getting it out is part of the experience. Then you start noticing the little design details. The faded brown-and-gold colourway features Lara silhouettes across it; there's a lovely golden metallic D-pad, and the whole thing looks like something recovered from an ancient tomb. The D-pad itself reminds me of a lost coin or compass face, which is a nice touch.

Sources indicate that the metal D-pad disc did fall off once, but clipped back in fine. Do I expect that from a $120 controller? No, not really. Do I expect it from a $120 collectable controller where brand and design dominate? Yeah, probably.

In a recent development, I like that 8BitDo hasn't gone overboard with the branding; it feels like a well-made piece of gaming hardware, with the Tomb Raider design integrated rather than simply plastered on. The buttons are solid black, the sticks feel responsive, and the controller has a reassuring weight. The triggers have a nice solid feel, not too light but with a little flick as they snap back into place if released.

Then there's the stand, which I think is my favourite bit. The controller sits snugly in place, with a matching decal underneath, and it looks like you're slotting an ancient stone artefact into some sort of polar key and lock from the games. A soft orange LED glows when the controller charges, and suddenly I've got a little Tomb Raider shrine on my desk. I didn't think I needed one, but here we are.

Industry observers note that what's clever about the design is that it gets at the look and feel of Tomb Raider without relying on Lara's face everywhere. The original games had such a distinctive visual identity: those angular environments, sandstone ruins, green foliage and Lara's turquoise costume, and it's a look that's stuck with me. The Ultimate 3 is more of a celebration of Lara across the series, but the colours, materials and little relic-like details bring back some of that atmosphere.

In a recent development, the less expensive Pro 3 Bluetooth Gamepad takes a more direct route back to the original game. Its design is inspired by the Lost Valley, with a jungle and ancient temple scene, and the charging stand picks up that weathered stone look. It's a different approach, and I rather like it. There's something about the Pro 3's shape, too, that reminds me of the old PS2 DualShock. It's lighter and a little more plasticky than the Ultimate 3, but still comfortable to hold, with a nice tactile feel to the buttons.

Recent findings suggest that this is the one I'd look at if I were playing on Switch 2, especially if you want to revisit the Tomb Raider: Definitive Survivor Trilogy on Nintendo's console. It's a good-looking pad; the Lost Valley artwork is lovely, and the included stand gives it personality when you're not playing. It's also a capable modern controller, with TMR sticks and Hall-effect triggers, so you don't feel like you're buying it purely for the artwork.

But I keep glancing back at the Ultimate 3. The Pro 3 is perfectly good and arguably has a stronger connection to the original 1996 game, but it doesn't quite have the same sense of occasion. Its unboxing is much more straightforward, and I never thought I'd say this, but I'd happily pay the extra for the Ultimate 3 packaging. The fact that the controller feels better made is a bonus.

I've always thought of collectable gaming hardware as something that looks nice in a display cabinet but doesn't necessarily earn its place in everyday use, and I think that's what has surprised me most about these two pads. The Ultimate 3 has made me reconsider my somewhat cynical approach to collectable controllers, as it’s a gamepad I actually want to use, but I also like having it on my desk, and the whole thing was designed with that in mind.

In a recent development, switch 2 players shouldn't feel left out. The Pro 3 is a lovely alternative, and if you're particularly fond of the original Tomb Raider, there's a lot to like about its Lost Valley design. But if you're after the full treasure-hunter experience, the Ultimate 3 is the one that has me reaching for my wallet. And that's something I really didn't expect to say about a controller.

Visit the 8Bitdo Tomb Raider website for more info.

Sources indicate that ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

#102999. Latest Update: Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts
