#102888. Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (912 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (912 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended).
  • But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s vital to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about fresh plasma as an anti-aging elixir.
  • Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s vital to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about fresh plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

“It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she claims.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

Industry observers note that what that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

Sources indicate that “There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”.

Sources indicate that about 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

And the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

In a recent development, “So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” says Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In a recent development, in the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

Sources indicate that at first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she says.

Part of the reason for this, says Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, says Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be notable to find out for whom this works.”.

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

“I would call this a phase 1 study,” states Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by James Brittain (unless stated otherwise).

Canadian studio Sid Lee Architecture has created a curved-glass hotel that takes cues from the burgeoning wine region of Ontario.

The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

“The Clayfield was conceived as a new hub for Niagara-on-the-Lake, a place where wine culture and hospitality find a home,” Martin Leblanc, architect and co-founding partner of Sid Lee Architecture, told Dezeen.

“Its layered contours, rounded geometry and rhythmic wood elements translate the surrounding vineyard landscape into a building that celebrates the region’s contribution to Canadian winemaking.”.

The hotel was conceived as a pavilion set in the emerging townscape between vineyards and the Clayfield Commons housing development on an agricultural road.

The curved form allows access and connection to its surroundings in multiple directions.

“The hotel acts as a threshold between these typologies, connecting the vineyard and the denser village-like development around it,” Leblanc said.

“Its exterior wood elements recall the rhythm of the vine rows, the layered concrete refers to the clay soil and the reflective glass registers the changing light, sky and seasons.”.

The studio said that the organic, natural flow of a hotel is essential to the lasting success of the design.

Working back and forth between the architecture and the interior design, the studio laid out spaces to progress from public to private and back again, integrating moments for visitors to discover the landscape.

“As visitors approach and circulate around the building, it frames changing views of the vines, the plaza and the emerging neighbourhood,” Leblanc said. “The lobby acts as a gateway to the vineyard, while the rooftop terrace reconnects the hotel experience with its broader surroundings.”.

Meanwhile, the staircase acts as a connector, transition and centrepiece between the plaza, lobby and upper levels.

“Inside, we chose a palette that speaks to the natural beauty of Niagara’s wine country: walnut panelling, concrete, dark amaranth-coloured leather, greige limestone and woven fabrics,” Leblanc remarked, calling out the limestone registration desk chiselled from the Niagara Escarpment and the restaurant’s curved bar that resembles the shape of the building.

With mostly Teknion furniture, each space represents a season of the vineyard, from spring in the lobby to winter in the guest rooms with more quiet, reserved furnishings that complete the rooms that fan out from the rounded concrete strata.

It has been revealed that founded in 2009, Sid Lee Architecture has six offices across North America and Europe. The studio previously remodelled its own offices in an I.M. Pei office building, overhauled the interiors of the iconic Fairmont Queen Elizabeth Hotel and created an artisan-inspired workplace for video game designers – all in Montreal.

7 Common Misdiagnoses for Hidradenitis Suppurativa (HS)

📅 14 Feb 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Greatist

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a skin condition that often gets caught up in a case of mistaken identity in a lineup of suspects.
  • With their host of bumps, rashes, flakiness, or scales, skin conditions can sometimes be tricky to diagnose.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is a skin condition that often gets caught up in a case of mistaken identity in a lineup of suspects. Specifically, people confuse HS for some more common conditions.

With their host of bumps, rashes, flakiness, or scales, skin conditions can sometimes be tricky to diagnose. That’s because they often share common symptoms or have symptoms that overlap with or mimic those of another skin issue.

It has been revealed that so, what exactly is HS? It’s a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in friction-prone and sweaty areas, where your skin can be sensitive. These lumps can form interconnected tracts underneath your skin (aka “tunneling”) that may become irritated or even infected.

Knowing how the symptoms of HS compare with those of other inflammatory skin conditions can help you advocate for the correct diagnosis and care, which is crucial for staving off disease progression.

Here are 7 conditions that HS commonly gets mistaken for.

Industry observers note that HS isn’t rare — it affects up to 4% of the population. But by comparison, acne vulgaris affects more than more than 9% of people worldwide. Sometimes HS can be mistaken for acne simply because acne is more common. But these two conditions are quite different.

According to recent reports, acne typically shows up as papules, pustules, or nodules, which are commonly called zits or blemishes. Acne most often appears on your face but can also affect your back, chest, arms, and buttocks. It occurs when your sebaceous glands have a hypersensitivity to circulating androgens (like testosterone).

It has been revealed that by comparison, HS most often appears in sweat- and friction-prone areas, such as your armpits or groin. It occurs when hair follicles become blocked — though more research is needed to learn what causes these blockages.

Recent findings suggest that acne conglobata (AC) is a rare but intense form of nodulocystic acne. With AC, the cysts and nodules connect under your skin, and this can lead to infections and scarring. Since AC features a “tunneling” effect that may appear similar to HS, many people confuse these two otherwise distinct conditions.

Sources indicate that one key difference? HS often appears in areas that are subjected to friction from skin-on-skin contact or chafing. AC, on the other hand, can appear anywhere on your body. To further complicate things, many people with HS also have AC, and some research suggests a link between the two conditions.

Industry observers note that A cyst is a fluid-filled sac. Cysts have many possible causes, including injuries and minor infections. They often go away on their own, but some may require treatment.

HS bumps can resemble cysts — but HS is an ongoing inflammatory condition.

Industry observers note that an ingrown hair happens when a strand of hair anywhere on your body grows into your skin instead of out. Ingrown hairs commonly occur after shaving, waxing, or tweezing. After hair removal, a tiny new hair can curl inward, creating a bump (often called a razor bump).

Industry observers note that sometimes people confuse HS bumps for ingrown hairs — especially since HS often occurs in places where hair removal is common, such as the armpits and bikini area. Another confusing factor is that HS develops from blocked follicles. However, the cause of the blockage in HS is more complicated than an ingrown hair.

Folliculitis is inflammation of hair follicles, usually caused by a bacterial infection. The inflamed hair follicles show up as small bumps and can look like ingrown hairs.

People commonly mistake HS for folliculitis because the conditions often occur in the same skin areas.

Mild folliculitis tends to go away on its own with at-home treatment, though more severe forms may require antibiotics. HS, on the other hand, is a chronic condition.

According to recent reports, A boil (also called a furuncle) is a bump filled with pus. The bump develops from a bacterial infection, often of a hair follicle. The infection causes a buildup of immune and skin cells, which leads to the formation of the bump. A carbuncle is a cluster of boils.

People often confuse HS with boils. However, boils are the result of an infection, and proper treatment typically resolves the matter. Meanwhile, the boil-like bumps of HS often require ongoing treatment.

Herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the herpes simplex virus. It demonstrates up as painful sores or blisters.

Recent findings suggest that since herpes often affects the genital area and HS occurs around the groin or bikini line, people may confuse the two conditions. But while herpes can be spread through direct contact, HS is not contagious.

According to recent reports, other skin conditions can mimic HS, and vice versa. But a misdiagnosis can lead to an incorrect treatment that won’t actually ease your symptoms or slow the condition’s progression. This is true for other skin conditions as well.

That’s why, if you have symptoms of any of the above conditions, you should talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can properly diagnose your concerns and find the right treatment strategy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”.

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”.

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

Recent findings suggest that “With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an important part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”.

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”.

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” mentioned Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”.

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos rolled out earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the tech giant’s website.

#102882. Tech Report: Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 17 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1084 w)

Tech Report: Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

📅 17 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1084 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people.
  • It has been revealed that in fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

It has been revealed that in fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas, tells SELF. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

Recent findings suggest that if you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller notes, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

In a recent development, at the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

It has been revealed that an allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller states, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.).

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran claims. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

Industry observers note that if you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication right about now. Pollen counts are rising, and antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Recent findings suggest that both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.).

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller indicates to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

In a recent development, if the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran indicates. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller notes. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

Sources indicate that if you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to office pod brand Framery, when companies resize or move, desks and meeting-room furniture often aren’t deemed “worth the cost of moving” and are discarded during the process.

Framery explained that the EU and US discard 11 million tonnes of furniture a year.

Specifically, the brand points to a study for the European Environmental Bureau, which found that in the EU, 80 to 90 per cent of office furniture is burned or landfilled.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency, in the US, less than one per cent is recycled.

Framery aims to tackle this concern with its office pod subscription service, presenting a more environmentally-friendly alternative to disposing of office furniture when a lease runs out, for example.

“The ‘fast furniture’ trend means 80 per cent of furniture ends up in landfills,” mentioned Framery’s chief design officer, Joonas Vartola. “We wanted to create a pod that’s part of the solution, not the problem.”.

“Framery pods are built for heavy use, keeping them in the field for tens of thousands of sessions and out of landfills,” Vartola added.

For example, if there’s an increase in staff and more pods are needed, or if an office’s layout changes.

The scheme covers the full range of its signature line pods, from one-person phone booths to meeting pods.

According to Saija Serpola, managing director and founding partner at IR Partners, using the pods has enabled increased flexibility and reduced financial risk when investing in additional office furniture.

“We can terminate, increase, or change the solution as our organisation develops.”.

Framery pods are built from mono-materials, including steel, aluminium, glass and PET.

Recent findings suggest that “Our pods with heavy-duty, high-quality materials engineered to withstand wear and tear,” stated Vartola. “It’s all about reducing waste, from design to decades of use.”.

As part of the scheme, when a change is required, the pods are dismantled, shipped and rebuilt, rather than discarded into landfill.

In a recent development, according to Framery, each pod is designed for disassembly, with all parts replaceable and recyclable. This includes everything from interior panels, glass, upholstery, carpet, ventilation units and seals.

During refurbishment, each pod is restored to as-new condition and delivered to its next office with a lifetime warranty.

“That is a manufacturing question before it is a commercial one, and it is settled years earlier, on the drawing board.”.

To learn more, visit Framery’s website.

The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.

Central to the building’s new function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.

“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts said.

“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”.

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be unveiled on 26 November.

Sources indicate that comprising three reuse projects, RIAS mentioned this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “notable conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

Can You Actually ‘Boost’ Your Metabolism?

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism.
  • Recent findings suggest that the truth?
  • Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Few bodily processes are as focused on and as misunderstood as metabolism. It seems like just about everyone wants to “boost” or “speed up” their metabolism in the hopes of burning more calories and, as a result, losing body fat. In reality, this is not an easy task, but you wouldn’t know that from the countless TikToks claiming it’s as simple as taking a shot of apple cider vinegar, hopping into an infrared sauna, or braving a cold plunge.

Recent findings suggest that the truth? Many of these supposed hacks don’t have much research backing them up, and the ones that do won’t meaningfully move the needle when it comes to your weight. Improving your metabolism actually boils down to a few basic tenets that aren’t flashy or sexy but can have long-term benefits for your overall health and well-being. We’ll get into all that, but first, a little background on what your metabolism even is.

Metabolism is commonly thought of as the mechanism that controls your weight. Having a “fast” metabolism means your body burns calories rapidly, making it easier to maintain or lose weight, while having a “slow” metabolism means you gain pounds more easily and have a harder time taking them off. This isn’t wrong, per se, but it doesn’t tell the whole story. Your metabolism is the way your body turns food into energy. This energy is then used to power your heart and lungs, build and repair tissue, regulate hormones, and perform other critical functions.

Put more succinctly, “metabolism is all the chemical processes that keep our body alive and functioning,” explains Jonathan Gabison, MD, an assistant professor of family medicine at the University of Michigan who is board-certified in obesity medicine.

For example, about 20% of the energy your metabolism provides goes to your brain, building neurotransmitters and keeping signals going, so having an efficient metabolism is critical for cognitive health.

It has been revealed that in short, yes. Your metabolism is influenced by loads of factors, from genetics and age to weight. But that doesn’t mean your metabolism is fixed. It’s actually highly modifiable, claims Shebani Sethi, MD, a clinical associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University and the founding director of the world’s first academic metabolic psychiatry clinical program.

That mentioned, taking shots of apple cider vinegar in the morning or picking up “metabolism-boosting” supplements won’t do the trick. Research shows that improving your metabolism requires consistent long-term habits. Here are five that can make an impact.

Recent findings suggest that every time you move your body, it burns calories and raises your metabolism—both during the moment and for a period afterward. Think of your metabolism like a pie: Two thirds of the energy you use every day is devoted to keeping you alive (that’s your basal metabolic rate), and the rest goes toward digesting food and moving your body. Being more active is the most straightforward way to up your metabolism. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.

This can include dedicated exercise, like a jog, hike, or workout class. (The CDC recommends that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity physical activity a week.) But it also extends to all the movement you do outside of formal exercise, known as NEAT (non-exercise activity thermogenesis). Increasing your daily step count, prioritizing physical hobbies like gardening and walking your dog, or even taking on more household chores and grocery runs all count toward upping your overall movement.

Strength training helps build and maintain muscle mass. Muscle tissue is metabolically active, which means sustaining it burns more calories than maintaining fat tissue. Therefore, having more muscle mass will give your metabolism a slight boost.

By strength training you’re also improving your overall health. For instance, since muscle tissue uses the majority of the glucose in your bloodstream, more muscle mass can increase your body’s capacity to use glucose and help prevent blood sugar spikes. Plus, research has shown that having more muscle helps improve insulin sensitivity, including in individuals without diabetes.

Those same CDC exercise guidelines suggest including at least two days of strength training every week. That can include body-weight moves like push-ups and lunges; lifting weights with dumbbells, kettlebells, barbells, or cable machines; or utilizing resistance bands. Dr. Gabison states what’s most vital is being consistent with your exercise routine, so it’s best to choose workouts you’re likely to stick with. And remember, if you’re just starting out, it’s important not to push yourself too hard early on and risk injury.

Protein is having a major moment right now. While things may be getting a little out of hand (hello, protein popcorn), consuming sufficient amounts of high-quality protein has well-established benefits for your metabolism. That’s because the nutrient is the building block of muscle, so eating enough of it helps support muscle growth and maintenance, especially if you’re resistance training.

Protein also has the highest thermic effect of all three macronutrients, meaning digesting it burns more calories than carbohydrates or fats. Plus, it’s the most satiating macro, so increasing your protein intake can help you feel fuller and fend off cravings, which may help with weight management.

In a recent development, however, balance is key. Sun Kim, MD, MS, a board-certified endocrinologist and associate professor of medicine at Stanford, claims doctors and health care providers have different viewpoints on how much protein is enough for optimal health. In her opinion, “most Americans eat plenty of protein without trying,” she says, cautioning that consuming excessive amounts won’t magically speed up your metabolism and could even worsen insulin sensitivity in some cases. So unless you’re extremely active, there’s no need to get hundreds of grams a day.

According to recent reports, for most healthy adults, the recommended dietary allowance for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. That means a 120-pound person needs roughly 43 grams of protein a day, which is about what you’d find in two four-ounce hamburger patties. If you incorporate some protein into every snack and meal throughout the day, you should easily hit the mark. That noted, some groups need more. People who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or highly active may need up to 2 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Older adults and those taking GLP-1s should also be mindful of their intake, as reduced appetite can lead to inadequate protein intake and muscle loss, particularly when coupled with reduced physical activity.

An often-overlooked habit for better metabolism is getting quality sleep. A lack of sleep dysregulates your metabolism, causing a cascade of issues, including worsened glucose management, more intense hunger the next day, and reduced energy expenditure. (Sleepy people are less likely to move their bodies.) When this happens consistently, it can lead to an increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Sleep also has an impact on hormones that can slow down the metabolism.

There isn’t a specific number of hours you should sleep each night, but research highlights that most adults do best with seven to nine hours of quality rest most evenings.

Recent findings suggest that prolonged stress keeps your cortisol (stress hormone) levels chronically elevated, which can break down muscle tissue and slow your metabolism. Constantly pulling out your hair can also disrupt your appetite-regulating hormones, triggering cravings that may prompt you to eat more. All of these things can affect your weight. Research demonstrates chronic stress can increase your risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and related cardiometabolic complications too.

There is, sadly, no quick fix for reducing stress, so some trial and error might be required to figure out what works best for you. Some places to start are doing yoga, meditating, practicing breathing exercises, going for walks outside, journaling, spending time with loved ones, engaging in relaxing hobbies, or starting therapy to talk through whatever is weighing on you.

According to recent reports, sure, supporting a healthy metabolism can increase the number of calories you burn and help with weight management. But it can also improve what’s known as your metabolic health, which encompasses measures such as blood pressure, cholesterol, insulin sensitivity, and total body fat. Having good metabolic health is essential for preventing chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease. The healthier your metabolism, the more calories you burn and the better your metabolic health.

Latest Update: 7 Places on the Body That Hidradenitis Suppurativa Can Appear

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Despite what Instagram and photo filters would have us think, no one has perfectly smooth skin over the entirety of their body.
  • Recent findings suggest that but hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is different.
  • HS lumps or bumps can form interconnected tracts underneath the skin that may become inflamed and infected, causing discomfort and pain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite what Instagram and photo filters would have us think, no one has perfectly smooth skin over the entirety of their body. We’re all prone to the occasional bump, rash, zit, or ingrown hair. These problems generally go away after the blocked follicle, clogged pore, or minor skin irritation resolves.

Recent findings suggest that but hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is different. HS is a chronic, progressive skin condition that typically appears as boil-like lumps in some of your most sensitive regions (and beyond).

HS lumps or bumps can form interconnected tracts underneath the skin that may become inflamed and infected, causing discomfort and pain. Although infections are often a part of HS, the disease itself is not an infection — it’s due to an ongoing inflammatory response in the body.

In a recent development, in addition to causing pain and discomfort, HS can be extremely frustrating and impact your self-esteem. Identifying HS correctly and early is crucial for getting optimal care, easing symptoms, slowing disease progression, and improving your mental health.

While we don’t know what exactly causes HS, genetic, environmental, and hormonal factors may play a role. Skin regions prone to HS include those where we sweat often and where friction is super common. Friction can occur from skin rubbing on skin, or where clothing can chafe or rub.

Here are seven areas of the body that are often impacted by HS.

Our underarms are packed with hair follicles and apocrine glands (aka, sweat glands). With HS, these follicles and glands may become clogged, and bacteria can start to grow, leading to the inflamed boil-like bumps of HS.

In a recent development, if you’ve ever gone for a run and come back with the dreaded armpit chafing, you’re all too familiar with how this area of the body can be prone to skin-on-skin friction or excessive rubbing from clothing. (Lookin’ at you, sports bra!) Friction and chafing can also cause an HS flare-up.

In a recent development, complicating matters is that some people shave or wax their armpits, and many understandably slather this region with antiperspirants or deodorants. These factors can also clog or irritate sweat glands and hair follicles.

The breasts, including underneath and even on the areolae (the area around the nipple), are a common place for HS to show up.

In a recent development, the breast area is a frequent spot for chafing from bras or other clothing. This chafing not only causes skin irritation — it can also trap sweat and bacteria on the skin. The areolae contain apocrine glands and hair follicles that can easily become infected. All these factors can contribute to an HS flare.

Industry observers note that research also points to sex hormones playing a role in HS, so a hormone shift or imbalance may also make breast tissue more prone to HS lesions. However, more research is needed on the connection between HS and hormones.

Recent findings suggest that no one can deny that the crotch becomes a sweaty area when life gets steamy, either from the weather, a workout, or both. It’s also a common area for clothing to rub against just from walking and everyday movements.

It has been revealed that as with other HS-prone areas, the groin and genital areas contain apocrine glands and oodles of hair follicles, all of which can become blocked as part of HS, leading to a flare. Speaking of hair down there, many people groom their pubic region, which can also lead to blocked hair follicles.

Again, hormonal shifts or imbalances may also play a role in why these sensitive areas can become hot spots for HS.

It has been revealed that the inner thighs are an extension of the groin area. Similarly, sweat also hangs out here, and it’s a common spot for chafing to occur from skin-on-skin friction, or from clothing rubbing and irritating the area.

Sources indicate that the entire buttocks area is also prone to HS in many people. Areas commonly affected include the anus, the butt crack, and the gluteal fold — or the crease where the buttocks meet the backs of the upper thighs.

Sources indicate that apocrine glands and hair follicles are abundant here, too. Sweat and other bacteria sources can also lead to HS infections. The buttocks are also subjected to pressure from sitting, which can lead to further irritation.

Industry observers note that although more research is needed, some studies suggest a link between HS and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). IBD is an umbrella term for conditions such as Crohn’s and ulcerative colitis. The potential links between HS and IBD may play a role in why the buttocks area is a common site for HS.

Although less common than in other areas, HS can also show up at the nape of the neck. This might be due to friction from clothing collars, jewelry, and other clothing or accessories. The neck is also a common site for sweat, which could block hair follicles in this area.

It has been revealed that if skin folds at the waist, or clothing waistbands (especially tight ones!) cause friction, it can lead to HS in the waistband area. As a result, HS lesions may show up on the abdomen, back, or sides.

HS tends to appear on some of the body’s most sensitive places, including the underarms, breasts, groin, and buttocks. These areas are prone to sweat, friction, and irritation from hair removal — all of which may contribute to an HS flare.

If you suspect you have HS, talk with a knowledgeable dermatologist who can give you a proper diagnosis and help you develop the right treatment and self-care plan to combat irritation and flares so you can feel more comfortable in your skin.

  • Architecture studio BIG has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.
  • Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, BIG designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.
  • Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.

Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, BIG designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.

Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s new Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.

The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.

The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,.

“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a latest development,” BIG partner Sören Grünert said.

“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.

“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”.

Recent findings suggest that the hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.

Here, projecting bays and set-back terraces will help to create privacy for the residents, whose homes will overlook a shared courtyard.

BIG used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.

The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.

Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.

BIG also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.

"All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the upcoming Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.
  • The beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes.
  • Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the new Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the upcoming Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

The beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the new Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks.

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

That last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

It has been revealed that in our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the massive deal.

In a recent development, A both bigger and smaller problem is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

That is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

According to recent reports, the architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

In a recent development, in recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same challenges that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

Sources indicate that to be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility complications – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many owners, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Brooklyn Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers.

That leaves only a deeper glitch, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Industry observers note that objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

It has been revealed that inside, as Rem Koolhaas once mentioned, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.
  • The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.
  • It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

In a recent development, with The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh says, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused Newly introduced Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the challenges that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

Recent findings suggest that “I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”.

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she says has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she mentioned.

The Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.

The 20×20 series, released to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a significant impact on the next 20.

With just 10 years between the start of their practices, Escobedo and Lanza Atelier represent two crests on a new wave of Mexican architecture that has brought regional references to the world stage and made adventurous but sympathetic interventions at home in Mexico City.

Escobedo was one of Lanza Atelier’s Alessandro Arienzo’s teachers at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and he and partner Isabel Abascal cite her as an inspiration whose success with kindred ideas has given them the confidence to pursue their vision.

They are becoming known for distilling complexity down to simple and pure gestures, whether in the appropriately snaking crinkle-crankle walls of their Serpentine Pavilion, inspired by the English countryside, their Cancun house with materials and forms drawn from sea snail shells, their Re-Source exhibition design that visitors could take home, or their hierarchy-challenging Family of 4 chairs, prompted by the arrival of their second son.

For Escobedo’s part, she identifies Arienzo and Abascal’s dedication to concept and process, which involves extensive research and testing, as key to their strength.

“Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous,” said Escobedo. “They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play that makes their architecture both thoughtful and joyful.”.

The Lanza story began in 2015, with toilets. Arienzo was approached by a client who, nearing the end of their bike path development in Mexico City, realised that they needed public bathroom facilities along the route. Arienzo suggested to Abascal, originally from Madrid, that they work on together on the project.

Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous. They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play.

Promptly, their collaboration turned one of architecture’s humblest structures into a nexus for meaning and care.

“We were exploring the scarcity of means and materials, but also the boundaries between inside and outside, and how to make something very simple like a toilet become something larger, like a meeting point and a resting space,” stated Abascal.

“And also how to blueprint for the future of public architecture that might not be very taken care of or maintained by combining landscape and construction.”.

The finished project features semi-open structures built from concrete blocks and filled with planting, creating a network of shaded resting points along the exposed track.

From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza. Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since].

Bamboo trees loosely divide the male and female toilets, but they share common sinks – a feature that Lanza Atelier pushed for as part of their vision for a space of respectful coexistence between all owners.

“It came out really naturally and fun, and simple,” remarked Arienzo. “That first interaction made Lanza happen because we needed to build a tech giant after that.”.

The nature of the collaboration pushed them to establish a distinct language from the get-go, adds Abascal.

“From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza,” she noted.

“Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]. We explored so many different options, and we were so opinionated about how it should be. We very rigorously really gave all the importance to designing a toilet.”.

As Escobedo identifies, Lanza Atelier’s work has a remarkable sense of play considering it lacks the colour, ornamentation or usual curlicues that would prompt association with the word.

Their use of materials is almost austere, in the sense that many of their projects have seen them hone in on just one material and push it to its limits, as in the local Sienna bricks of their Serpentine Pavilion.

Arienzo characterises this “extreme” approach as being “maybe a phase” more than a signature of the studio’s work. Instead, the key feature is how they arrive at the choice.

Industry observers note that “We pick materials because of where the project is or what we have close to the site,” Arienzo said. “We analyse what’s the best or least aggressive way to build [in that place], because, we always say, building is really violent.”.

Using fewer materials also allows them to focus more on questions of space, and makes it easier for their pavilions and installations, often demountable as a matter of principle, to find a second life.

“The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract,” said Abascal.

The main matter is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract.

That’s where the playfulness comes in, the designers identify, allowing them to dig into various elements, flip them, manipulate them and be curious about them.

“That, I think, is the playground,” adds Arienzo.

When asked what qualities each of the duo brings to the table that makes their work together so strong, Arienzo is initially flippant.

“I’m the bad cop,” he says with a smile.

But when the duo finally answers seriously, their responses do seem to reveal something about the alchemy going on behind the scenes.

It has been revealed that “I used to call Alessandro’s gaze towards the world ‘the laser eye’,” mentioned Abascal. “He is always pointing things out to me – mostly in our everyday lives, it’s things that the city creates and produces informally, but his laser eye applies to every context.”.

“And it’s not only something visual but has to do with how things are and are put together and solved.”.

For his part, Arienzo describes Abascal as the powerhouse behind Lanza’s ideas and concepts.

Industry observers note that “I think she gives a lot of meaning to the projects,” said Arienzo. “I think without this, I would just do soulless stuff. She connects the work with history, with literature, with art.”.

Lanza Atelier’s slate presently includes a house in LA to replace one destroyed by the wildfires, several projects in Mexico City and the design for the Expanded Tradition exhibition on contemporary Mexican craft at Qatari museum M7. When we speak, Abascal is on her way to the Canary Islands to conduct research on bird migration and pregnancy. It’s a patchwork that is idiosyncratically Lanza.

Neither Arienzo or Abascal seems to be the type to have a 10-year initiative – asked about professional goals, Arienzo replies that they’re more orientated towards taking better care of themselves and their children – but they identify housing, particularly collective housing, as the type of architecture they most want to work on.

They hope to do it within a global industry that demolishes less and values what’s already built more, and that learns from the original “sustainable architecture” of vernacular construction in places like Mexico.

The country has been in the spotlight in the last few years as one of the few in Latin America with a progressive government, and one whose president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has frequently had to stand her ground against its northern neighbour.

Asked about whether government policy has had any positive effect on architecture and related industries at home, Abascal and Arienzo’s good cop and bad cop come out.

“From architects of the older generation, our generation and the younger generation, I can feel a sense of optimism,” said Abascal.

“I feel a sense of doing nothing,” said Arienzo. “Claudia is way better than what there was before; I’m a leftie. But I think there should be many more competitions around housing in the city.”.

Both say they would like to see more public competitions in place of private developments, and that they would eagerly enter.

“Mexico City’s downtown is beautiful and it’s almost empty,” said Arienzo. “There isn’t a lot of density. I think it should be much more about that. Housing is a substantial issue and will be forever for these big cities.”.

Recent findings suggest that there is an ideal future for the architects, then. It’s one that would see the urban landscape of their home city benefit from the respect, creativity and serene beauty that is the Lanza calling card.

According to recent reports, to celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

Sources indicate that how do you remember the dimensions of a room you could barely see? Perhaps through the distance between footsteps, the sound of a door closing, or the way an echo travels down a corridor. Architectural drawings rely on measurements and spatial relationships, yet our memories of places rarely follow the logic of a floor plan. We remember routes, sounds, thresholds, and landmarks, often without knowing their exact positions or dimensions. Reconstructing a place from these fragments requires interpreting what people remember, what they have forgotten, and where their accounts disagree. The resulting representation carries both spatial information and the uncertainties of its sources.

The reconstruction of Saydnaya Prison in Syria, Hands-on Famagusta in Cyprus, and Memoria Cronotópica in Barcelona explore these questions under different circumstances: a prison whose interior was inaccessible, a city divided by conflict, and buildings that have disappeared. Across these different conditions, drawings and models become a way to investigate places beyond what can be directly observed or measured, bringing together spatial evidence that exists in memories, testimonies, and historical traces.

Reconstructing Architecture Through Sound.

Industry observers note that for years, independent investigators could study Saydnaya Prison from the outside, including through satellite imagery, but had no access to its interior. Inside the military prison north of Damascus, much of what could be reconstructed depended on the memories of people who had been held there.

Recent findings suggest that for years, independent investigators could study Saydnaya Prison from the outside, including through satellite imagery, but had no access to its interior. Inside the military prison north of Damascus, much of what could be reconstructed depended on the memories of people who had been held there.

In 2016, Forensic Architecture worked with Amnesty International to reconstruct the prison from the memories of five former detainees interviewed in Istanbul. Starting with a rough model based on satellite images and earlier written testimony, researchers developed the interior as survivors described cells, stairwells, and doors. The witnesses explored the rooms at eye level, corrected their proportions, and placed objects where they remembered them. Moving through the model sometimes brought back details they had never mentioned.

Some dimensions came from physical memories of the building. One survivor remembered the size of a hatch in his cell door because guards had forced him to push his head through it. Another estimated the dimensions of a cell by counting its floor tiles.

Some dimensions came from physical memories of the building. One survivor remembered the size of a hatch in his cell door because guards had forced him to push his head through it. Another estimated the dimensions of a cell by counting its floor tiles.

Industry observers note that sound provided another way to reconstruct the interior. Detainees were frequently blindfolded or kept in darkness, and speaking was prohibited. They became attentive to footsteps, doors, and noises traveling through water pipes and ventilation ducts. Audio investigator Lawrence Abu Hamdan gathered what the team called "ear-witness testimony," using simulated echoes and reverberations to help survivors recall the spaces they had occupied. These comparisons helped estimate the dimensions of cells, corridors, and stairwells.

Sources indicate that the investigation also documented how sound traveled through the prison's architecture. Pipes and ventilation ducts carried noises between spaces, while differences in echoes and reverberation helped survivors distinguish rooms and corridors they could rarely see. In his related work, Saydnaya (the missing 19dB), Abu Hamdan examined how enforced silence had intensified after 2011, including a 19-decibel reduction in the whispering levels remembered by survivors.

In a recent development, the accounts did not always agree. Witnesses had experienced Saydnaya under different conditions, so the team cross-referenced spatial and acoustic testimony, corrected discrepancies where possible, and documented those that remained. These differences could also reveal how individual prisoners had experienced and remembered the building. The resulting interactive model can be explored by location or by witness, bringing their accounts together within one reconstructed space.

The relationship between the model and the building changed in December 2024, when the fall of the Assad government made Saydnaya accessible to journalists, families, and investigators. Its interior could finally be examined directly, opening the possibility of comparing the reconstruction with the prison's physical dimensions. Yet the survivors' testimonies also preserved information about how they had experienced those spaces through darkness, sound, and enforced silence, details that a physical survey alone could not recover.
